passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, and I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke’” (verse 1). Moses is to be ready in the morning and come up alone. No one else may be seen anywhere on the mountain (verses 2-3).

“So Moses chiseled out two stone tablets like the originals. He rose early in the morning, and taking the two stone tablets in his hands, he went up Mount Sinai as the LORD had commanded him” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The calf story began in chapter 32 with the covenant broken. Here it ends with the covenant remade.

God will write the same words again. The covenant is not swapped for an easier one. God does not lower the terms to fit Israel's failure. He restores what was lost on its first terms, and he supplies the writing a second time.

There is one difference. The first tablets were ‘the work of God’ (32:16). This time Moses must cut the stone, and God will write on it. The Hebrew verb for ‘chisel’ is the root of the word for a carved image, the thing forbidden in the second commandment. After Israel's forbidden image, the only carving God asks for is two blank stones to receive his word.

God names the breaking of the tablets, ‘which you broke’, without a word of blame.

The mountain is closed more tightly than before. In chapter 24 Aaron, his sons and the elders went part of the way. Now Moses goes alone, and even the flocks are kept back. The people's sin has made the distance greater. One man stands between them and God.

Moses ‘rose early in the morning’. The people had risen early to sacrifice to the calf (32:6). Many details in this chapter answer chapter 32 in this way.
passages.later:
Moses tells it again in Deuteronomy. God said, “I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke; and you are to place them in the ark” (Deuteronomy 10:2).

Jeremiah promises a day when the writing will go deeper than stone: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).
passages.asks: God offered to write the same words a second time on new stone. Ask what you have broken that you think cannot be given back. And ask what it would mean to come to God in the morning with empty hands and a blank stone, and let him write.

passages.happening:
“And the LORD descended in a cloud, stood with him there, and proclaimed His name, the LORD” (verse 5).

“Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: ‘The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generations’” (verses 6-7).

“Moses immediately bowed down to the ground and worshiped. ‘O Lord,’ he said, ‘if I have indeed found favor in Your sight, my Lord, please go with us. Although this is a stiff-necked people, forgive our iniquity and sin, and take us as Your inheritance’” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Moses had asked, ‘Please show me Your glory’ (33:18). God promised to proclaim his name. Here he does it. Moses asked to see, and what he is given is mostly something to hear. God's glory is shown as his character.

These two verses are the Old Testament's own creed about God. No other description of him is quoted so often in the rest of the Old Testament. And they are spoken by God about himself, right after Israel's worst sin. The calf story does not end with Israel proving it is sorry. It ends with God saying who he is.

Each word carries weight.

‘Compassionate’ is rachum. It is related to the Hebrew word for a womb, and it speaks of tender care. In the Old Testament it is used almost only of God. It stands first.

‘Gracious’ is channun, kindness freely given and not earned. Moses has twice asked whether he has found favor. God's answer is that giving favor is what he is like.

‘Slow to anger’ is, word for word, long of nostrils. Hebrew pictures anger as hot breath from the nose. God's anger is real, and it takes a long time to rise.

‘Loving devotion’ is chesed, one of the great words of the Old Testament. It means love that keeps faith inside a relationship, even when the other side has failed. ‘Faithfulness’ is emet, what is firm and can be trusted. The word amen comes from the same root. God abounds in both.

‘Forgiving’ is a verb that means to lift or carry. To forgive is to carry the weight of a wrong away. And three words for wrong are named, iniquity, transgression and sin, which together cover guilt, rebellion and failure. God names himself as the one who carries all three.

Then the short, sober line. He ‘will by no means leave the guilty unpunished’. Mercy does not mean that God calls evil good. The list is balanced with care: a long line of mercies, then a brief word of justice. Love reaches ‘a thousand generations’. Judgment reaches three or four. In the Ten Commandments the order was the other way round, with judgment first (20:5-6). After the calf, God puts mercy first.

Moses' answer is to bow to the ground, and then to pray once more. He does not pretend about the people. He calls them stiff-necked to God's face, and asks for forgiveness for that very reason. And he says ‘our iniquity’. He counts himself among them.

Jewish tradition calls these verses the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, and recites them in prayers of repentance before and during the High Holy Days. The Talmud reads the name said twice, ‘The LORD, the LORD’, as meaning that God is the same merciful God before a person sins and after a person sins and repents.
passages.later:
The rest of the Old Testament keeps coming back to these words, and each writer takes what he needs. After the spies' report Moses prays them back to God (Numbers 14:18), and God answers, “I have pardoned them as you requested” (Numbers 14:20).

A psalm sings them: “The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (Psalm 103:8). Joel uses them to call the people home: “return to the LORD your God. For He is gracious and compassionate” (Joel 2:13). Nahum uses the other side, against a cruel empire: “the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished” (Nahum 1:3). And Jonah complains about them, because they meant that God would spare his enemies: “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger” (Jonah 4:2).

John says of Jesus, “We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). ‘Grace and truth’ most likely echoes the pair in verse 6, loving devotion and faithfulness.

Paul sees the two halves of the name meet at the cross, where God acted “so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).
passages.hard:
Does God punish children for their parents' sins?

The verse can trouble readers, and the Bible itself raises the question. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting children to death for their parents' crimes. Ezekiel says plainly, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20). Many critical scholars read those passages as a later correction of an older idea of shared guilt.

The note on Exodus 20:5-6 sets out how the words have been read, and the same readings apply here. The oldest Jewish answer, in an old Aramaic translation and in the Talmud, is that the verse applies to children who go on sinning as their fathers did. The matching words in 20:5 point the same way, since they speak of ‘those who hate Me’. Others note that three or four generations was the span of one household living together in the ancient world. So the verse describes how one generation's sin damages everyone under its roof, a pattern still seen in families. A third reading takes it of the shared life of a people, whose sins and their results carry forward in its history.

The proportion matters most. Mercy reaches a thousand generations. Judgment stops at three or four. The verse stands inside a proclamation whose main point is God's mercy. And Jesus refused the idea that a man was born blind because of his parents' sin: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

So this verse is never a curse on any family. It does not mean that God punishes a child for a parent's sin, or that anyone is doomed by where they come from. No one is bound by a parent's choices. Anyone, from any family, may turn to God and find his loving devotion.
passages.asks: God described himself, and mercy came first and at length. Ask which half of this name you find harder to believe: that God is this merciful, or that he will not call evil good. And ask what you would pray if you prayed, as Moses did, with these words in your mouth.

passages.t: The covenant renewed, and no other gods
passages.happening:
“And the LORD said, ‘Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will perform wonders that have never been done in any nation in all the world’” (verse 10).

God will drive out the peoples of the land (verse 11). Israel must make no treaty with them, “lest they become a snare in your midst” (verse 12). “Rather, you must tear down their altars, smash their sacred stones, and chop down their Asherah poles. For you must not worship any other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (verses 13-14).

Israel must not share their sacrifices or take their daughters as brides for its sons, or the sons will be led to their gods (verses 15-16). “You shall make no molten gods for yourselves” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Moses asked God to forgive and to take the people as his own. God's answer is, ‘Behold, I am making a covenant’. The covenant is renewed after it was broken, and the renewal rests on God's character, not on Israel's record.

The commands that follow are not a new law. They repeat duties from chapters 20 to 23, and above all the ones Israel has just broken. ‘You shall make no molten gods’ uses the very word for the molten calf (32:4).

The warnings look ahead to the land. Asherah was a goddess known from the texts of Ugarit, and her sign was a wooden pole or carved tree that stood at shrines. The danger was real and lasting. Inscriptions from about 800 BC, found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, bless people by the LORD and his asherah. They show that some Israelites later did join the worship of the LORD with hers, the very thing this chapter forbids.

Why no treaty? In that world a great king's treaty forbade his people to make alliances with other kings. Israel's king was the LORD. A treaty with the peoples of the land would be a betrayal of him.

The warning about marriage in verse 16 is about gods, not about blood. The text gives its own reason: the sons would be led to other gods. Rahab of Jericho and Ruth of Moab, both foreign women, were welcomed into Israel when they turned to Israel's God.

‘Whose name is Jealous’ can sound ugly to a modern ear. Jealousy is usually a fault, a sign of an insecure and grasping heart, and readers who say so should be heard. But the Hebrew word covers zeal as well as jealousy, and in the Old Testament God's jealousy is always that of a covenant partner. As the note on Exodus 20 says, it describes a husband's rightful passion for his marriage. A love that felt nothing when it was betrayed would be a lesser love. And this chapter sets God's jealousy inside a name that begins with compassion and grace.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy gives the same reason for the marriage law: “because they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4). It happened to the wisest of Israel's kings: “when Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4).

Ruth the Moabite shows the other road: “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16).
passages.hard:
Does the command to tear down altars give anyone the right to attack other people's worship today?

No. The command concerns Israel's own worship in its own land, at one point in its story, and it is set beside the warning that such worship would become a snare to Israel. It is not a charter for forcing other peoples anywhere else. The New Testament gives the church no such command.

These notes say nothing against any people, ancient or modern. The peoples named here are not a name for anyone living today, and this passage gives no one permission to hate or harm any people or to claim any land. The note on Exodus 23:27-33 faces the driving out of the nations at more length.
passages.asks: God calls himself jealous for his people's love. Ask what in your life competes with God for your first loyalty. And ask whether there is some small agreement you have made with it, a treaty that has become a snare.

passages.t: Feasts, firstborn, rest, and the words written
passages.happening:
“You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread”, in the month of Abib, “For in the month of Abib you came out of Egypt” (verse 18). The firstborn belong to God; firstborn sons are to be redeemed. “No one shall appear before Me empty-handed” (verses 19-20).

“Six days you shall labor, but on the seventh day you shall rest; even in the seasons of plowing and harvesting, you must rest” (verse 21). Israel is to keep the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Ingathering (verse 22). Three times a year all the men are to appear before God, “and no one will covet your land when you go up three times a year to appear before the LORD your God” (verses 23-24).

“The LORD also said to Moses, ‘Write down these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel’” (verse 27). Moses is there forty days and forty nights without bread or water, and the words of the covenant are written on the tablets (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
These commands repeat much of 23:12-19. The note on that chapter explains the three feasts and the farming year. Here they are given again, after the calf, as the rhythm of a people who will worship the LORD and no other.

Abib is an old name for the spring month when the barley ripened. After the exile it was called by the Babylonian name Nisan.

Two details are new. The Sabbath is to be kept ‘even in the seasons of plowing and harvesting’, the two times of year when a day's work mattered most. Rest is an act of trust.

So is the promise of verse 24. Three times a year the men would leave their farms and borders unguarded to appear before God. God promises that no one will covet their land while they are away.

The firstborn belong to God in memory of the night Israel left Egypt (13:14-15). A firstborn son was redeemed, bought back with an offering. Jewish families still keep the ceremony, called pidyon haben, when a firstborn son is a month old. The law about the young goat in its mother's milk, repeated in verse 26, is explained in the note on chapter 23.

What was written on the tablets? Verse 28 says it was ‘the words of the covenant’, the Ten Commandments, and verse 1 says God would write the same words as before. Most readers take the tablets to hold the Ten Commandments of chapter 20, with verses 10 to 26 as a restating of duties Israel had just broken. Some scholars, since the German writer Goethe in 1773, have argued that the laws of this chapter were themselves an older list of ten commands about worship. Those who hold that view count the ten in different ways, and no list is agreed.

Moses fasts forty days and forty nights, as he had the first time. The covenant is whole again.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy settles who wrote on the second tablets: “And the LORD wrote on the tablets what had been written previously” (Deuteronomy 10:4).

Jesus too fasted “forty days and forty nights” (Matthew 4:2), a link of theme rather than a stated fulfillment.

Mary and Joseph kept the law of the firstborn for Jesus, “as it is written in the Law of the Lord: ‘Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord’” (Luke 2:23).
passages.asks: Israel was to rest even at harvest, and to leave its land unguarded to worship. Ask where trusting God would cost you something you can measure. And ask what you bring when you come before him, since no one was to come empty-handed.

passages.t: The shining face, and the veil
passages.happening:
“And when Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the Testimony in his hands, he was unaware that his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD” (verse 29). “Aaron and all the Israelites looked at Moses, and behold, his face was radiant. And they were afraid to approach him” (verse 30).

Moses calls them back. First Aaron and the leaders come, then all the people, and Moses gives them everything the LORD told him (verses 31-32).

“When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face. But whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with Him, he would remove the veil until he came out” (verses 33-34). When he came out, he told the people what he had been commanded, and they saw his shining face. “So Moses would put the veil back over his face until he went in to speak with the LORD” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
The last time Moses came down with tablets, he found a calf and broke them. This time he comes down with the covenant restored, and his face shines.

He does not know it. The light is not his own. It comes ‘from speaking with the LORD’. Moses asked to see God's glory. Now, without knowing, he carries some of it on his face. God's glory changes the one who is near it.

The people are afraid, as they were afraid of God's voice at the mountain (20:19). The fear is answered in the same way. Moses calls them near, and God's word comes to them through him.

Notice the order, because it is often missed. Moses speaks to the people with his face uncovered. They see the light and hear the words together. He puts the veil on afterward. Then it becomes his regular practice: in before the LORD with no veil, out to the people with no veil while he speaks God's words, and then the veil until he goes in again. The Hebrew word for this veil is used nowhere else, and the text does not say what it looked like or why he wore it.

The Hebrew verb for ‘shine’ is related to the word for a horn. Horns and rays both stand out from what they belong to. The Latin Bible called the Vulgate translated the word as ‘horned’, and that is why some European art, most famously Michelangelo's statue in Rome, shows Moses with horns. In its setting the meaning is clear: his face shone.

So the long story of the calf ends. God is again speaking with his people through his servant, and the tabernacle can now be built.
passages.later:
The priests' blessing asks for what Moses received: “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:25).

When Jesus was transfigured on a mountain, “His face shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2), and Moses himself was there. Moses' face shone with a glory that was not his own. The voice from the cloud said of Jesus, “This is My beloved Son” (Matthew 17:5).

Paul reads this passage closely in 2 Corinthians 3. He grants that the covenant written on stone “came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses” (2 Corinthians 3:7), and argues that the Spirit's work has greater glory still. He takes up verse 34: “whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16). And he says that believers, “who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image” (2 Corinthians 3:18).
passages.hard:
Paul says Moses wore the veil to keep Israel from seeing the end of a fading glory, and speaks of a veil over the heart when Moses is read. Is that what Exodus says, and does it show contempt for the Jewish people?

Exodus does not say why Moses wore the veil, and it does not say that the shine on his face faded. Paul's words about ‘what was fading away’ (2 Corinthians 3:13) translate a Greek word that can mean to fade, to be brought to an end, or to be set aside. As the note on 2 Corinthians 3 says, Paul seems to be reading the whole story in the light of what came after: the glory of Sinai was real, but it was not meant to be the last word. Interpreters differ on how he reached the detail. Some think he drew it from the repeated veiling. Others think he meant that the veil shielded a stiff-necked people from a glory that would have judged them.

Paul then uses the veil as a picture of a covering over the mind and heart that keeps a reader from seeing where the Scriptures lead. He had read Moses that way himself for years. He says the veil is ‘taken away’ whenever anyone turns to the Lord, and the same could be said of any reader, of any people.

This must be said plainly, because these verses have been misused. For centuries some Christians used ‘the veil’ to look down on Jewish people, to mock them as blind, and to justify contempt and worse. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. Paul calls the old covenant glorious. He speaks as a Jew, of his own people, whom he loved: “I am an Israelite myself” (Romans 11:1). Nothing in Exodus 34, and nothing in Paul's reading of it, gives anyone a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people.

And in Exodus itself the veil is not a mark of blindness at all. The people see Moses' shining face every time he brings them God's word. The story is about a God who came back to his people after their worst sin and spoke with them again.
passages.asks: Moses did not know that his face was shining. Ask whether time with God has changed you in ways that others can see and you cannot. And ask what covers your own heart when you read the Scriptures, and what it would mean to turn to the Lord and have it taken away.
